title: 2 Chronicles 32:9–19
context: While Sennacherib is attacking Lachish, his servants come to Jerusalem to challenge the people’s trust, accuse Hezekiah of deceiving them, mock his removal of the high places, and claim that no god has ever delivered a people from Assyria. Letters insult the LORD, the God of Israel, and messengers shout in the Jews’ language to frighten those on the wall, speaking of the God of Jerusalem as one of the gods made by human hands. Chronicles condenses the longer speeches given in 2 Kings 18:17–35 and 19:9–13 and in Isaiah 36–37, and it does not name the Rabshakeh. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the passage as shared ground: the enemy’s words aim to separate God’s people from trust in him, and the LORD is not one god among many.

verses.text: After this, Sennacherib king of Assyria sent his servants to Jerusalem, (now he was attacking Lachish, and all his forces were with him), to Hezekiah king of Judah, and to all Judah who were at Jerusalem, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Sennacherib sending servants to Jerusalem while he attacks Lachish. The threat reaches the city through messengers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scene as the beginning of a contest over trust (compare 2 Kings 18:17). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as setting up the Assyrian taunts.

verses.text: Sennacherib king of Assyria says, “In whom do you trust, that you remain under siege in Jerusalem?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Sennacherib asking in whom the people trust as they remain under siege. The question goes to the heart of faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the question as unintentionally raising the central theme of the crisis. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a challenge to trust in the LORD.

verses.text: Doesn’t Hezekiah persuade you to give you over to die by famine and by thirst, saying, ‘The LORD our God will deliver us out of the hand of the king of Assyria’?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the claim that Hezekiah is leading the people to death by famine and thirst. Fear is used to undermine faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the taunt as an attempt to separate the people from their king and from God. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as calculated propaganda.

verses.text: Hasn’t the same Hezekiah taken away his high places and his altars, and commanded Judah and Jerusalem, saying, ‘You shall worship before one altar, and you shall burn incense on it’?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Assyrians twisting Hezekiah’s removal of the high places into a charge against him. Truth is distorted to confuse the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the taunt as misunderstanding worship at one altar as God commanded (compare Deuteronomy 12:13–14). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a deliberate attempt to sow doubt.

verses.text: Don’t you know what I and my fathers have done to all the peoples of the lands? Were the gods of the nations of those lands in any way able to deliver their land out of my hand?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Sennacherib boasting of what he and his fathers have done to all peoples. Past victories fuel his arrogance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the boast as forgetting that every victory lies under God’s rule. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as pride resting on human achievement.

verses.text: Who was there among all the gods of those nations which my fathers utterly destroyed that could deliver his people out of my hand, that your God should be able to deliver you out of my hand?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Sennacherib asking which god has delivered any people from his hand. He places the LORD among the idols.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the question as the fatal error of treating the LORD as one god among many. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the boast that God will answer.

verses.text: Now therefore don’t let Hezekiah deceive you nor persuade you in this way. Don’t believe him, for no god of any nation or kingdom was able to deliver his people out of my hand, and out of the hand of my fathers. How much less will your God deliver you out of my hand?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Sennacherib urging the people not to believe Hezekiah, since no god could deliver them. Doubt is pressed hard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the taunt as an open challenge to God’s power. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as pride that goes before a fall.

verses.text: His servants spoke yet more against the LORD God and against his servant Hezekiah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Sennacherib’s servants speaking yet more against the LORD God and Hezekiah. The insults multiply against God and his king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the blasphemy as directed ultimately against God himself. Both traditions commonly read the verse as heightening the tension before God’s response.

verses.text: He also wrote letters insulting the LORD, the God of Israel, and speaking against him, saying, “As the gods of the nations of the lands, which have not delivered their people out of my hand, so shall the God of Hezekiah not deliver his people out of my hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Sennacherib writing letters insulting the LORD and comparing him to the gods of the nations. The attack is put in writing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the insult as aimed at God himself (compare the letter Hezekiah spreads before the LORD in 2 Kings 19:14). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a direct challenge to God’s honor.

verses.text: They called out with a loud voice in the Jews’ language to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall, to frighten them and to trouble them, that they might take the city.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the messengers shouting in the Jews’ language to frighten those on the wall. Fear is used as a weapon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the tactic as psychological warfare aimed at ordinary people. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing how intimidation seeks to weaken faith.

verses.text: They spoke of the God of Jerusalem as of the gods of the peoples of the earth, which are the work of men’s hands.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Assyrians speaking of the God of Jerusalem as one of the gods made by human hands. They confuse the Creator with idols.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the comparison as the central error the following verses answer. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as preparing for the LORD’s deliverance.
